newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: War-torn Kabul braces for battle against cold.
newsitem.headline: War-torn Kabul braces for battle against cold.

text.p: Kabul saw its first fall of snow on Monday night, adding cold to the list of woes facing the city's hard-pressed population.
"The people are not equipped to face winter. They don't have any money to buy wood and coal," said Jean-Luc Paladini of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) in Kabul.

Temperatures in Kabul can fall to 20 degrees Celsius below freezing (minus 4 Fahrenheit) at night. After four years of continuous civil war, much of the city's population is under-nourished and housing is frequently inadeqate.
"We are seeing long-term chronic malnutrition," said Joerg Stoecklin of the ICRC.

The combination of malnutrition and cold is making life extremely difficult for most of the poverty-stricken people of the capital. Aid workers expect the situation to deteriorate further as the winter progresses.

"This winter could be worse than the previous ones. People have been selling more and more of their posessions to buy food and they are running out of things to sell," said Bridget Fenn, a nutritionist with Action Contre le Faim (Action Against Hunger) in Kabul.

Employment opportunites in Kabul are few and far between, and even those with jobs are having difficulty affording enough food, and will have even greater difficulty finding the money to buy heating fuel during the winter.

"We have had inflation of 400 per cent since the beginning of the year," said Paladini. "Many people can't afford to buy wood. A civil servant earns 130,000 Afghanis ($6.50). How can a family of six with one person who works afford to buy food, clothes, wood, medicines .... They are all expensive."
The ICRC estimates that one family needs seven kg (15 pounds) of wood per day for cooking and heating.
"With wood at its current price that means that enough wood for one month costs almost twice a civil servant's monthly salary," said Paladini.

Action Contre le Faim (ACF) estimates that a basic food basket for a family of six for a month costs 500,000 Afghanis ($26.50). "There is this big gap between income and how much they need for survival," said Fenn.
She expects the gap to increase. "You need more food in the winter, because you expend more energy just trying to keep warm.

"We are expecting an increase in cases of acute respiratory infection during the winter, and if the nutritional status is already poor, the infection will have a greater effect than on a well-nourished person," Fenn said.
The quality of Kabul's housing is also causing concern. The United Nations agency Habitat estimates that as much as 50 percent of the housing stock has been destroyed or severely damaged.
Paladini paints a bleak picture of the living conditions of many Kabulis. "Many houses have no (glass in the) windows, just plastic sheeting, and plastic does not provide any insulation," he said.
In the past, although winter brought its own hardships, it also brought a lull in the factional fighting. However, Afghan watchers in Kabul say winter will have less effect this year.
"In the past the factions relied on supply routes that were often blocked in the winter, but now they have roads they can use all year," said one.
He pointed out that last winter saw some intense military activity. "The Taleban managed to advance all the way from (the southern city of) Kandahar to Kabul between November and February last year."
